title: Refractory ventricular tachycardia storm associated with severe hypokalemia in Fanconi syndrome
case_prompt:
A 52-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department after a syncopal episode. Her medical history included Fanconi syndrome with renal tubular acidosis (stage IV chronic kidney disease) and primary biliary cirrhosis; she had no known cardiovascular disease. She had taken naproxen and ibuprofen for catarrhal symptoms. En route, telemetry showed ventricular ectopy, and the initial ECG demonstrated polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, a QTc of approximately 500 ms, and no evidence of ischemia.

Over the next 7 hours, she had continuous runs of polymorphic VT and ventricular fibrillation requiring approximately 150 external defibrillations. Episodes were initiated by short-coupled premature ventricular complexes of multiple morphologies and by sinus bradycardia; sinus rhythm returned only briefly.

Initial laboratory studies showed:  
• Potassium 2.5 mmol/L  
• Bicarbonate 13 mmol/L  
• Chloride 122 mmol/L  
• BUN 31 mg/dL  
• Creatinine 3.77 mg/dL  
• Magnesium 2.5 mg/dL  
• Calcium 8.5 mg/dL  

Toxicology and coagulation tests were unremarkable. Thyroid studies revealed low T3 and low TSH with a normal free T4. Cardiac biomarkers remained negative. Bedside echocardiography showed a preserved ejection fraction with no wall motion abnormalities, pericardial effusion, or structural heart disease. Chest radiograph was unremarkable.

Treatment included intravenous amiodarone, lidocaine, potassium, magnesium, calcium, propranolol, isoproterenol, benzodiazepine sedation, propofol infusion, and rapid ventricular pacing at 130 beats/min, with only transient improvement. Despite 150 mEq of IV potassium repletion, her serum potassium fell to a nadir of 1.7 mmol/L. When the arrhythmia burden became intermittent, venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation was initiated, and a left stellate ganglion blockade was performed, after which arrhythmia burden decreased and no further defibrillation shocks were required.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Acute myocardial ischemia was considered but deemed unlikely — “as evidenced by the negative successive cardiac biomarkers, as well as preserved EF and absence of wall motion abnormalities seen on initial evaluation with echocardiography.”  
2. Underlying structural heart disease was excluded — “Bedside echocardiography demonstrated a preserved ejection fraction and no wall motion abnormalities, pericardial effusion, or evidence of structural heart disease.”  
3. Congenital long QT syndrome was considered but deemed less likely — “it was deemed less likely, however, since congenital QT syndromes present infrequently as VT storm.”  
4. Acquired QT prolongation due to hypokalemia was identified as a primary contributor — “the prolonged QT interval seemed to be a consequence of severe hypokalemia secondary to Fanconi syndrome.”  
5. Viral myocarditis was evaluated via biopsy but found to be mild — “minimal interstitial lymphocytic inflammation with edema.”  
6. A primary genetic arrhythmia syndrome was considered given a TRDN variant but was regarded as unlikely — “Since our patient was heterozygous for a previously unreported variant in TRDN, a primary genetic basis for her arrhythmias is extremely unlikely.”
